introduction: Caius Martius is a formidable defender of Rome who openly despises the citizens whose safety he preserves. Hunger and demands for political representation expose the gulf between his martial idea of honour and the people's claims upon the state. Victory abroad promises advancement at home, but public office requires forms of persuasion he resents. His mother's ambition, his friendship with Menenius and his rivalry with the Volscian Aufidius draw him into conflicts where military courage offers no simple guide to loyalty.

fullSynopsis.text: Rome's hungry citizens rise against the patricians, naming Caius Martius as their fiercest enemy. Menenius tries to defend the Senate through a fable comparing it to the nourishing belly of a body, but Martius meets the protest with open contempt. The people have nevertheless gained tribunes to represent them, including Sicinius and Brutus. War with the Volscians interrupts the conflict. Martius admires their commander Aufidius as the adversary most worthy of him. At home, his mother Volumnia celebrates the dangers that bring honour, while his wife Virgilia fears for his safety.

At Corioles, Martius rallies retreating Romans and follows the enemy alone through the gates. Emerging bloodied, he helps capture the city, then joins Cominius's battle and fights Aufidius, who is rescued by other Volscians. Martius refuses an exceptional share of the spoils, but accepts a horse and the honouring name Coriolanus. He also asks freedom for a former host taken prisoner, though he cannot recall the man's name. Aufidius, repeatedly defeated by him, determines that future revenge need not follow the rules of honourable combat.

Rome greets Coriolanus with acclaim, and the Senate chooses him for the consulship. He resents the required appeal for popular votes, refusing to display his wounds as payment for approval. Under Menenius's guidance he performs a contemptuous version of the ritual and initially secures the citizens' voices. Sicinius and Brutus, fearing both his hostility to popular rights and the loss of their own power, encourage the voters to withdraw consent. Challenged before confirmation, Coriolanus denounces the distribution of free corn and the authority of the tribunes. They accuse him of treason and call for his immediate death; his armed supporters get him away.

Menenius obtains a formal hearing. Volumnia urges her son to use political accommodation as he would a military stratagem, and he reluctantly promises to speak mildly. The tribunes deliberately provoke his anger with an accusation of seeking tyranny. He erupts, and they pronounce banishment with the crowd's support. Declaring that he banishes Rome in turn, Coriolanus leaves his family and friends. He travels disguised to Aufidius's house in Antium, offering either his throat or his service against his own country. Aufidius embraces the former enemy and shares command of the Volscian army with him.

The allied commanders advance upon Rome, overturning the tribunes' confidence that the city prospers without its defender. Citizens try to distance themselves from his expulsion, while Menenius and Cominius blame those who drove him out. Aufidius becomes jealous as the army's devotion transfers to Coriolanus and prepares to exploit a future fault. Cominius fails to soften Coriolanus, and Menenius is dismissed despite their former intimacy. Then Volumnia, Virgilia, Valeria and Coriolanus's young son arrive. Volumnia argues that destroying Rome would destroy his honour and force his family to choose between him and their country. She asks reconciliation that can honour both sides.

Coriolanus yields to his mother, warning that her victory for Rome may prove fatal to him. He negotiates peace and returns with Aufidius rather than entering Rome, where the women are welcomed as saviours. In Antium, Aufidius organizes conspirators and accuses him of surrendering victory to women's tears. Coriolanus insists that the treaty benefits the Volscians, but loses restraint when called a tearful boy and boasts of his destruction of Corioles. The crowd recalls its dead, and the conspirators kill him despite the lords' demand for a hearing. Aufidius then professes sorrow and helps carry the body away to a mournful military march.

acts.label: ACT I
acts.summary: Citizens protesting hunger threaten Martius, whom they regard as an enemy of the poor. Menenius defends patrician government with his fable of the belly, while Martius insults the crowd and condemns the grant of elected tribunes. News that the Volscians are in arms draws him to war under Cominius; he relishes the chance to confront Aufidius. Volumnia praises the honour won through danger, in contrast with Virgilia's anxiety. At Corioles, Martius forces retreating soldiers to rally, pursues the enemy alone through the gates and survives being shut inside. After the city's capture he refuses rest, joins Cominius and drives Aufidius back despite Volscian assistance. Offered a special share of the spoils, he declines unequal reward, but accepts a horse and the name Coriolanus. His request for a captive host's release reveals a moment of pity. Aufidius resolves to defeat him by craft if open combat cannot succeed.

acts.label: ACT II
acts.summary: Menenius quarrels with Sicinius and Brutus over Martius's character, while Volumnia welcomes news of victory and wounds that may support a claim to office. Coriolanus returns amid public celebration but finds praise uncomfortable. Volumnia wants the consulship for him, whereas the tribunes fear that his advancement will extinguish their authority. At the Capitol, Coriolanus leaves rather than listen as Cominius recounts his military deeds. The Senate approves him for consul, but popular assent is still required. He protests the custom of wearing humble clothes and displaying his wounds, then undertakes it with marked reluctance. The citizens grant him their votes despite his scornful manner. After he leaves to prepare for formal confirmation, the tribunes emphasize his refusal to show his scars and his hostility to the people's freedoms. They encourage the voters to revoke their choice and blame the tribunes themselves for having recommended him.

acts.label: ACT III
acts.summary: Sicinius and Brutus halt Coriolanus on his way to confirmation, announcing the people's changed judgment. His fury turns the dispute into an attack on free corn, popular political judgment and the tribunes' existence. They charge treason and attempt to arrest him; when they call for his death from the Tarpeian rock, he draws his sword and his supporters drive the crowd back. Menenius persuades both sides to accept a lawful hearing. At home, Volumnia argues that tact need not betray honour and presses Coriolanus to perform humility for the safety of family and state. He agrees reluctantly. The tribunes prepare the crowd's responses and plan to provoke him. At the hearing, their charge that he seeks tyrannical power breaks his promised mildness. They banish him under threat of death if he returns. Coriolanus answers with curses, declares that he banishes them, and leaves Rome.

acts.label: ACT IV
acts.summary: Coriolanus takes leave of his distressed family and friends, refusing Cominius's offer to accompany him. Volumnia and Virgilia confront the tribunes with anger over the expulsion. Intelligence of Rome's divisions reaches the already preparing Volscians. Disguised in poor clothing, Coriolanus enters Aufidius's house in Antium and withstands the servants' attempts to eject him. Revealing his identity, he offers to fight his banishers or be killed by the enemy he has so often defeated. Aufidius joyfully accepts him and shares command, reversing their longstanding rivalry. In Rome the tribunes boast of tranquillity until repeated messengers and Cominius confirm an invasion led by Coriolanus himself. Alarmed citizens disclaim responsibility while his friends blame the expulsion. As Roman territories yield, Aufidius observes that the army idolizes his new partner. He resents being overshadowed and plans to use Coriolanus's eventual accounting for the campaign against him.

acts.label: ACT V
acts.summary: Cominius reports that his appeal for mercy has failed; Menenius nevertheless tries and receives a harsh dismissal. Coriolanus then confronts his mother, wife, son and Valeria, struggling to place revenge above family affection. Volumnia argues that either side's victory would ruin those closest to him and urges a peace honourable to Rome and the Volscians alike. When the women kneel and prepare to leave unanswered, he yields, recognizing the danger this concession creates for himself. Rome celebrates the women's return and the army's withdrawal. In Antium, Aufidius arranges a conspiracy and depicts the peace as a betrayal of a certain conquest. Coriolanus presents the treaty and spoils as an honourable settlement, but Aufidius's insults provoke him into recalling his devastation of Corioles. The crowd turns hostile and the conspirators kill him before a hearing. The lords demand mourning, and Aufidius joins the soldiers carrying him away to a dead march.
